CASAMA DATA SCIENCE

Will anyone behome when it arrives

Casama helps housemates coordinate parcels. This analysis studies 99,441 real online orders to learn when parcels are late, so the app can warn housemates earlier.

THE PROBLEM

Parcels arrive when nobody is in

In a shared home, a missed delivery means a failed attempt, a trip to the courier, or a cash on delivery payment nobody can cover. If Casama knows a parcel is likely to be late or early, housemates can plan who receives it.

CONTEXT

Life in a shared home

Casama is for people who share a living space: college students in dorms, young professionals renting a condo, and families coordinating errands. Their daily coordination usually happens in one busy group chat, where important details get buried.

Questions housemates ask every day

Is anyone home right now?
Can someone receive my Shopee or Lazada parcel?
Who has the extension cord?
Did anyone buy drinking water?
The faucet is leaking. Who reports it?

A parcel day, step by step

  1. A parcel is on the way. A housemate logs it with the courier and the expected arrival. It is cash on delivery.
  2. Everyone is asked. Housemates are marked available by default and tap unavailable if they will be out all day.
  3. A conflict is spotted. If every housemate is unavailable, the buyer gets an alert and can plan a backup.
  4. Someone receives it. A housemate claims it, pays the courier (paluwal, or spot me) and the app records who owes what.
  5. Where the data helps. If the parcel is likely to be late or early, the app can ask for availability sooner.

Context and scenarios come from the Casama project proposal.

OUR PROCESS

From raw file to app feature

01

Ask

Can we tell early which parcels will be late, so housemates can plan who receives them.

02

Collect

Downloaded 99,441 real orders from Kaggle. Eight columns, all timestamps and a status.

03

Clean

Kept delivered orders with a date, removed impossible durations and extremes. 96.3% of all orders survived.

04

Explore

Charted delivery time, lateness, seasons, seller speed and promised windows.

05

Model

Trained on 2017 and tested on 2018, so the model is judged on months it never saw.

06

Apply

Turned each finding into a Casama parcel board feature.

DATA QUALITY

Cleaning the data

2,965 orders were never delivered, and 740 more were removed as impossible or extreme. Cancelled and unavailable orders are kept out of the lateness analysis on purpose.

EXPLORATORY ANALYSIS

What the data shows

Half of all parcels arrive within 10.2 days. One in ten takes more than 22.9 days.

Estimates are padded. Only 7.9% arrive late and the typical parcel lands 12 days before the promise.

Lateness is not constant. March 2018 hit 21% late, against 1% in the calmest month.

The best early warning is the seller. When shipping takes 7+ days, 23% of parcels are late, versus 4% when it ships within a day.

Short promises break most: 17% late when under 10 days were promised, versus 5% for 30+ days.

Orders cluster in the afternoon. Parcels bought then often arrive while housemates are at class or work.

Volume and lateness rise together (correlation 0.56). Busy months overload sellers and carriers.

A fast seller means a median of 7.2 days in total. A seller who takes 7+ days to ship means 19.0 days.

The dark mass sits below the line: most parcels beat the promise. The thin cloud above the line is the late 8%.

Seller handoff days link most to lateness (0.22). The promised window links weakly (-0.07). Hour and weekday barely matter.

PREDICTION

Can we tell which parcels will be late

A gradient boosting model was trained on 43,285 orders from 2017 and tested on 52,450 orders from 2018, so it is judged on months it has never seen.

At purchase

AUC 0.592

Barely better than guessing. Only the promised window and the month are known at this point.

After the seller ships

AUC 0.649

Adding the seller handoff time helps. Flagged parcels are late 20.4% of the time, 2.2 times the 9.1% base rate, and the alert catches 30.7% of all late parcels.

WHAT WE LEARNED

Five takeaways

  1. The seller matters more than the courier. Handoff time was the strongest signal (23% late when slow).
  2. Averages hide the risk. The median parcel is 12 days early, yet some months hit 21% late.
  3. Time of day and weekday do not predict lateness. We tested them and they added almost nothing, which saved us from a false story.
  4. Predicting lateness is hard. Even with the best signal, AUC reached 0.649. Honest results beat impressive ones.
  5. Split by time, not at random. A random split would have looked better and been less honest about future months.
USE IN CASAMA

From findings to the app

FindingCasama feature
Slow seller handoff predicts latenessParcel board shows a "might be late" flag once a parcel is logged as shipped late
Short promised windows break most oftenParcels with tight estimates ask housemates for availability sooner
Lateness peaks in busy monthsPeak season banner: confirm who can receive parcels this week
Orders cluster in the afternoonSuggest the receiver who is usually home at that hour from presence history
LIMITS

What this does not prove

  • The data is Brazilian marketplace orders from 2016 to 2018, not Philippine couriers. It shows the method, not local delivery times.
  • It has timestamps only. There is no courier, payment type or COD amount, so COD behaviour is not analysed.
  • The model is modest. Late parcels are hard to predict from timing alone, so alerts are a nudge, not a guarantee.
  • 2018 contained unusual spikes in February and March that the 2017 training data did not show.
GLOSSARY

Definition of terms

AUC (Area Under the Curve)
A score from 0.5 to 1 for how well the model ranks parcels from safe to risky. Pick one late and one on time parcel at random: AUC is the chance the model gave the late one the higher risk. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect.
Base rate
The share of all parcels that are late, with no model involved. In the 2018 test data it is 9.1%.
COD (Cash on Delivery)
Paying the courier in cash when the parcel arrives. In Casama a housemate may need to front this cash.
Correlation
A number from -1 to 1 showing how closely two measures move together. 0 means no link, and values near 1 or -1 mean a strong link. A link does not prove one thing causes the other.
Decile
One tenth of the parcels. We rank parcels by predicted risk and split them into ten equal groups, where 1 is the safest and 10 is the riskiest.
EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis)
Looking at the data with summaries and charts before modelling, to find patterns, errors and questions worth asking.
Estimated delivery date
The date promised to the customer when the order was placed.
Gradient boosting
A prediction method that builds many small decision trees one after another, where each new tree corrects the mistakes of the ones before it.
Late parcel
A parcel delivered after its estimated delivery date.
Lift
How many times more often the flagged parcels are late than an average parcel. A lift of 2 means twice as often.
Mean and median
The mean is the average. The median is the middle value when everything is sorted, so a few very slow parcels do not distort it.
Model
A program that learns patterns from past orders and uses them to estimate whether a new parcel will be late.
Outlier
An extreme value, such as a delivery that took 200 days. We removed these before analysis.
Permutation importance
A way to see which signals the model relies on. Shuffle one signal and measure how much the model's accuracy drops. A bigger drop means a more important signal.
Precision
Of the parcels the alert flags, the share that really are late.
Recall
Of all the parcels that really are late, the share the alert catches.
ROC curve (Receiver Operating Characteristic)
A chart of the share of late parcels caught against the share of on time parcels wrongly flagged, as the alert threshold changes. The area under it is the AUC.
Seller handoff days
The days between the purchase and the seller giving the parcel to the carrier.
Signal (feature)
A measured fact the model can use, such as the promised days or the seller handoff days.
Time based split
Training the model on older orders (2017) and testing it on newer ones (2018), so it is judged on months it never saw. A random split would look better but be less honest.
Source: Customer Order Delivery Dataset on Kaggle. Code in the analysis folder.
